title: Earth, sky, heaven, then the verse
hookLine: Om bhur bhuvah svah isn't in the Rig Veda's verse. it's the doorway: earth, the space between, the sky
carry: stand in all three worlds, then pray
tomorrow: what did a king ask a man who knew the Gayatri?

lines: BOOK THREE, HYMN SIXTY-TWO, VERSE TEN.
OM BHUR BHUVAH SVAH: NOT THERE.
A DOORWAY IN FRONT OF THE HOUSE.
cards: Open the Rig Veda to book three, hymn sixty-two, verse ten. Run a finger along the line, looking for the words that so often come first when the Gayatri is chanted: Om bhur bhuvah svah. They aren't there.
The verse begins tat savitur varenyam. The opening sits outside it, like a doorway built in front of a house. Today: the words before the Gayatri, and why they're said.

teach.h: NOT IN THE RIG VEDA'S TEXT.
teach.b: In daily recitation the Gayatri is often framed. First comes Om, the sacred syllable. Then three short words: bhur, bhuvah, svah.

They're called vyahritis, utterances. They aren't part of the Rig Veda verse; they come from the practice of reciting it, and from other Vedic texts that talk about them. One is the Taittiriya Upanishad.
In paraphrase: bhur, bhuvah, suvar, these are the three utterances, and a teacher named Mahachamasya made known a fourth, mahas. Then it lays them out like a map. Bhur is this world, the earth.
Bhuvah is the space in between. Suvar is the world beyond. And mahas is the sun.

So before a person asks the sun to stir their thoughts, they first name where they stand: the ground, the air, the sky. That's the teaching in the frame. In Hindu prayer you don't ask from a small corner.
You place yourself inside the whole of things, earth under your feet, the heavens over your head, and only then turn to Savitr.
Many teachers read it that way: whatever you're carrying, an exam, a fight at home, gets said from the middle of three worlds.
Om, then the three worlds, then the verse.

teach.h: EARTH, THE SPACE BETWEEN, THE SKY.
teach.b: So when someone says the Gayatri goes Om bhur bhuvah svah, tat savitur varenyam, they're describing how it's chanted, a living tradition of its own.

teach.h: STAND IN ALL THREE WORLDS, THEN PRAY.
teach.b: The text and the recitation are both real. One begins at the verse, the other at the doorway in front of it.

how: In daily recitation, Hindus who chant the Gayatri may begin with Om and the three vyahritis, bhur bhuvah svah, before the verse itself; traditions vary on further additions.

games.q: what does “the gayatri in context” mean?
o: the verse, with Om and three worlds said before it
the verse translated word by word into English
the verse chanted the same way in every single home

s: om bhur bhuvah svah is the first line of the Rig Veda verse
the verse begins tat savitur varenyam; the frame comes from recitation.
the Taittiriya Upanishad adds a fourth utterance, mahas
and it calls mahas the sun.
chanting the frame before the verse is a mistake
it's how the verse is recited in practice; the text and the recitation simply begin in different places.

games.q: you're about to recite the verse, framed. what comes right after Om?
games.why: bhur bhuvah svah: earth, the space between, the sky. only then the verse to Savitr.

practice: Before the sit itself, stand at its threshold for three out-breaths, saying silently here, then between, then beyond, or bhur, bhuvah, svah if you pray. Then step through and rest, letting the breath come and go on its own.
When the mind wanders, come back to the doorway, take the three breaths again, and step through once more.

wordCard.voice: The Gayatri in context. In recitation, the verse is framed by Om and three utterances: earth, the space between, and the sky beyond. The Rig Veda's verse itself begins at tat savitur. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: an utterance; the name for bhur, bhuvah, svah, the words said before the Gayatri.

carryVoice: Your line: stand in all three worlds, then pray. Earth, the space between, the sky, and then the verse. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.5 (bhur, bhuvah, suvar, and mahas; this world, the middle space, the world beyond, the sun)
